elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Rewritten 14.2.2: "PB may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to SFJ". The gating conditions (SFJ having paid/incurred $60 million of Development Costs; pre-first-Regulatory-Approval window) are deleted, so the election is unconditional. There are no Order Forms in this co-development structure, so "the Agreement" is the full covered scope. The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present: false" is a naming artefact — our party is styled "PB", not one of the generic Customer aliases — and is contradicted by the operative text.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to SFJ" replaces the redacted [***] notice period; 30 days is at (not above) the preferred ceiling and the notice is expressly written.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: "in which case SFJ will refund to PB, pro rata, any amounts prepaid by PB to SFJ under this Agreement, if any, for the period after the effective date of termination." The words "pro rata" are express (not merely inferred from a post-termination period), the payer is the counterparty, and the trigger is PB's convenience termination. The 300% Development Cost exit payment that would have negated any net refund is deleted.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: New 14.2.11: "SFJ shall have no right to terminate this Agreement for convenience during the Term." Term is defined at 1.1.185/14.1, so the trigger is not undefined. Retained SFJ exits are event-conditioned, not convenience: 14.2.6 requires a Change of Control of PB and 14.2.10 requires a JSC/Executive-Officer deadlock under Section 5.2.4; "in its sole discretion" in each is discretion to invoke a triggered right, not an at-will right, so neither contradicts 14.2.11.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: The rendered notice period is thirty (30) days, which is outside the literal 60–90 day fallback band (it is more favourable to us, but the fallback element is not literally satisfied). Immaterial here because the preferred level is complete.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the redline deletes the 300% Development Costs exit payment and adds no substitute fee, so no early-termination fee survives in 14.2.2 to be capped. The retained Approval Payment sentence is contingent on PB electing to continue development and actually obtaining Regulatory Approval, not an exit charge.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: 14.2.11 removes any SFJ convenience right during the Term entirely, which is stronger than confining it to term end; the surviving SFJ rights (14.2.3, 14.2.6, 14.2.10) are event-triggered.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: with no SFJ convenience right under 14.2.11, there is no convenience notice period to set.

reasons: Preferred level is position-complete in operative language: unconditional PB election, 30 days' written notice, express pro-rata refund of prepaid amounts, and an express bar on SFJ convenience termination during the Term.

The failing regex "Customer convenience termination present" is a party-alias artefact (our party is "PB"); substantively the operative sentence grants the convenience right, so the mechanical failure does not defeat coverage.

Edits stay inside the checklist: only the gating sentence, the redacted notice period and the 300% exit payment are removed. Removing the 300% penalty is necessary, not surplus, because a mandatory exit payment of 300% of Development Costs would contradict the pro-rata-refund element and the rule's "leave on notice without penalty" standard.

Deleting the trailing credit "and reduced by the amount previously paid by PB to SFJ pursuant to this Section 14.2.2" is a conforming change that avoids a dangling reference to a payment that no longer exists; it is not cosmetic surplus.

Favourable and unrelated language survives: the ARTICLE 6 Approval Payment continuation, the Section 6.2 adjustment and Section 6.7 Buy-Out carve-out remain in 14.2.2; 14.2.6, 14.2.10 and their payment formulas and the Section 5.2.2.2 cross-reference to 14.2.10 are untouched and are consistent with 14.2.11.

Diligence point (verify, does not currently defeat the finding): the deleted sentence framed the 300% payment as consideration "in exchange for purchasing the Trial Data Package ... as set forth in Section 11.1.1.4". Confirm Section 11.1.1.4 does not itself cross-refer to a payment "pursuant to Section 14.2.2"; if it does, conform that reference or add a short clause stating that on a 14.2.2 termination the Trial Data Package transfer is governed by, and consideration determined under, Section 11.1.1.4, to avoid a dangling cross-reference.

Optional tightening if SFJ pushes back on the deleted consideration: rather than reinstating a percentage exit payment, fall back to the playbook cap (60–90 days' notice with an early-termination fee not exceeding three months' fees) as already offered in the margin comment.
